context_candidates.text:
Poverty reduction is especially difficult in economies affected by conflict and institutional weakness, which typically face compounding challenges even after the conflict has subsided (Corral et al. 2020; Federle et al. 2024; Korn and Stemmler 2025; Novta and Pugacheva 2021; World Bank 2025b). Conflict destroys assets and disrupts livelihoods, whereas poverty fuels grievances and weakens the capacity of the state to prevent violence (Corral et al. 2020).

These challenges are compounded by the current global environment, in which economies dependent on energy imports and economies directly affected by conflict face the weakest growth prospects (World Bank 2026c). Furthermore, when a population grows quickly, the economy must expand even more quickly to deliver the same level of improvement in per capita welfare.

context_candidates.text:
Poverty reduction is especially difficult in economies affected by conflict and institutional weakness, which typically face compounding challenges even after the conflict has subsided (Corral et al. 2020; Federle et al. 2024; Korn and Stemmler 2025; Novta and Pugacheva 2021; World Bank 2025b). Conflict destroys assets and disrupts livelihoods, whereas poverty fuels grievances and weakens the capacity of the state to prevent violence (Corral et al. 2020).

These challenges are compounded by the current global environment, in which economies dependent on energy imports and economies directly affected by conflict face the weakest growth prospects (World Bank 2026c). Furthermore, when a population grows quickly, the economy must expand even more quickly to deliver the same level of improvement in per capita welfare.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

context_candidates.text: After decades of progress, global extreme poverty is projected to rise That poverty is now concentrated in economies where progress has stalled has profound implications for the outlook on extreme poverty. Because the population is also growing most rapidly in these same economies, the rising share of the global population in these economies is pulling the global poverty rate upward, even if national rates do not worsen. The stalled reduction in poverty may not merely be a temporary setback.6 If per capita growth in these economies continues at the pace observed over 2015–24, the global extreme poverty rate and the number of people living in extreme poverty will increase by 2030 (refer to figure 1.9). This would represent an unprecedented reversal of the decades-long decline in the global number of the extreme poor.

metadata.section: Gains in global poverty reduction could be reversed in coming decades

context_candidates.text: Poverty rates in many low-income economies, particularly those in a fragile and conflict- affected situation, are projected to decline only marginally.8 These same economies are projected to experience substantial population growth (refer to figure 1.10).9 Thus, it is the growing population in economies with high poverty rates, not the rising poverty rates, that give these economies greater weight in the aggregate poverty rate and that is driving the projections of rising global poverty rates. Fragile economies that are involved in conflict are at the center of this pattern. Economies such as the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Niger, Sudan, and the Federal Republic of Somalia combine some of the highest current poverty rates with some of the most rapid projected population growth.

context_candidates.text: The countries with high populations of poor people are on the list because of large populations or because of high poverty rates, or both. For example, India is among the top nine economies by poor population not because of a high extreme poverty rate, but because it is the most populous country in the world. Whereas India’s extreme poverty rate has decreased substantially over the last 15 years, poverty rates have either stagnated or increased in the remaining eight economies. These statistics are subject to uncertainty, however. In some of these economies, such as Afghanistan and the Federal Republic of Somalia, no survey data exist, and poverty estimates must therefore be imputed (Mahler et al. 2026). In others, such as the Republic of Y emen, the last survey with relevant data is several years old, and estimates must be extrapolated forward.

The differential price shock adjusts the real growth rates faced by households based on their food and energy expenditure. Growth is downgraded among households that have above average food and energy exposure, while it is revised upward for the rest to match the overall mean growth in the baseline. With these price shock assumptions, the number of people living in extreme poverty in 2026 is estimated at 813 million people, slightly below the 817 million in 2025.
